entries.name: companion-identity-not-derived-from-the-source
entries.claim: The companion transaction and line identities are a pure function of the stock-count source record ids. Deriving them from anything else -- here, from fresh randomness -- means the kernel mints a companion identity nothing can recompute, which is the copies-rather-than-derives defect `purchasing-sales-v1-plan.md` section 7.16 measured. SCOPE, narrowed on review: the kill is observed at the HEADER read-back, which runs before the line identities are independently compared, so this entry holds the header half at full strength and the line half only by construction. `source-line-companion-column-never-written` holds the line half. Kill sets are measured within the three `companion derivation` tests this command runs.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

entries.name: companion-revision-not-the-contract-initial-value
entries.claim: REWRITTEN ON REVIEW, around the corrected invariant. The companion is a newly created entity row, so it takes the compiled optimistic-revision contract's `initialValue: '1'` -- the same revision the generic mutation interpreter gives every create. The earlier version of this entry asserted the OPPOSITE, that the companion should inherit `sourceRevision + 1` so the two rows matched, and the review was right that this overloads the optimistic-revision field with lineage it does not carry: at source revision 9 it created a brand-new transaction at revision 10. This mutation restores that behaviour and the read-back refuses it.

entries.name: source-companion-column-never-written
entries.claim: The posted transition is where the source's companion transaction identity is written. Writing null there instead of the derived identity leaves a posted stock count whose companion column is still empty -- the source posts, the movements land, and nothing records which transaction they belong to. That is the silent-until-reconciled failure this packet's Band A declaration is about. The mutation writes `NULLIF($11, $11)` rather than deleting the assignment, because deleting it leaves the bound parameter unreferenced and PostgreSQL then refuses the statement with 42P18 -- a red, but not this red, and an entry whose kill dies for the wrong reason certifies nothing.

kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

entries.name: source-line-companion-column-never-written
entries.claim: Line-level companion identity is written per source line, not implied by the header. Writing null instead still satisfies the update's own row count -- the guard is `IS NULL` and the row stays null -- so only the read-back catches it. This is the vacuity vector where a write reports success and the fact does not hold. `NULLIF($5, $5)` keeps the bound parameter referenced, for the reason recorded on `source-companion-column-never-written`.

entries.name: reviewed-source-companion-must-be-null-fence-removed
entries.claim: The kernel does not ADOPT a companion identity it did not write. Replacing the fence with whatever is stored makes it do so. Measured, the posting is still refused -- the line check catches it further down -- so what the fence buys is the IDENTITY of the refusal: with it the operator is told the companion is the problem -- the refusal every pre-derivation stock count meets -- and without it they are sent to a line that is fine. NARROWED ON REVIEW: this holds non-adoption and the refusal's identity. It does NOT establish that the kernel is the only reachable WRITER of a companion column, which it is not -- generic draft-transaction creation and stock-count relation mutation remain open, filed as `companion-writers-not-closed`. It dies alone: the two posting tests are unaffected because their stored value is null either way.

entries.name: family-roster-transaction-type-repointed
entries.claim: The companion transaction's type comes from the EXECUTING family's own role binding, which the entry point resolved by `(capabilityId, familyId)` and which `#post` now carries rather than reselecting by role. Repointing the `count` role's declared type changes what the kernel writes for an initial count while leaving a correction alone, and the projection test compares both roles as ONE value so neither masks the other -- the correction the review asked for. It dies alone: only that test posts an initial count and reads its companion type.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: each role companion type comes from its own family role binding

entries.name: companion-business-key-not-derived-from-identity
entries.claim: The companion transaction's business key is derived from the derived identity, so it is unique whenever the identity is. `inventory_transaction_number` is `tenantEnvironmentCaseInsensitiveUnique`, so a fixed number lets the FIRST companion in a tenant write and makes every later one impossible -- the projection test posts an opening count and then a correction, and the correction cannot get a companion at all. MEASURED, AND NOT WHAT WAS FIRST DECLARED: the collision surfaces as INVENTORY_POSTING_IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT naming a natural effect race, because the savepoint's 23505 handler predates the kernel writing a companion and attributes every unique violation to a movement identity. The red is real and attributable to this mutation; the DIAGNOSIS the kernel prints is wrong, and that is filed as `companion-key-collision-misreported-as-effect-race` rather than repaired here.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: a natural effect identity was claimed by a different posting

entries.name: companion-derivation-namespace-moved
entries.claim: Companion identity must be STABLE, not merely deterministic, because it is the join a reconciliation reader recomputes against already-posted counts. Moving the namespace yields a derivation that is still pure and still deterministic, so write and read-back agree and the kernel's own read-back passes -- it recomputes with the function it wrote with. Only the golden vectors catch it. The two vectors are now compared as ONE value, so the transaction half no longer masks the line half; the review was right that sequential assertions measured only the first. It dies alone: every other assertion compares the kernel against the same derivation and moves with it.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: both companion derivations must be stable across releases

entries.name: legacy-stock-count-digest-recomputed
entries.claim: A stock-count receipt written before companion derivation carries a version-3 digest computed from CALLER-authored companion ids. This kernel derives them, so it cannot reproduce that digest and must refuse to try. Recomputing it instead produces a value that disagrees with what is stored, and the mismatch surfaces as the ordinary 'already names another posting' idempotency conflict -- sending an operator to hunt a conflicting posting that does not exist, when the real cause is a contract change. Migration 0016 is what makes this a rule rather than a preference: a writer keeps its version 'until their own digest input changes under a versioned migration', and 0022 is that migration. The control is scoped to the legacy-receipt test by name pattern, and the claim is scoped to match.

kills.name: stock-count legacy receipt: a receipt written before companion derivation is refused for its own reason
kills.expected: the refusal must name the contract change, not an ordinary key conflict
